{"result":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a general-purpose, multi-paradigm language that prioritizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1][2]. Its syntax resembles C++, yet it forgoes a garbage collector [2].

Graydon Hoare began developing Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored the project from 2009 [2]. The language was first released publicly in 2010, with version 1.0 following in 2015 [2].

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran permit unchecked pointer arithmetic [3]. Java offers a managed alternative, performing runtime bounds and dereference checks [3].

Beyond memory safety, Rust's design also draws on functional ideas, including immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].

Rust asks developers to master stricter compile-time rules, but in return it delivers memory safety without giving up low-level control.

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran permit unchecked pointer arithmetic [3]. Java offers a managed alternative, performing runtime bounds and dereference checks [3].

Beyond memory safety, Rust's design also draws on functional ideas, including immutability, higher-order functions, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].
